title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TACA.

title: Deep Q-network path planning with stratified sampling and prioritized replay
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been widely adopted for mobile robot path planning in unknown and complex environments. However, existing DRL-based approaches suffer from two main limitations: sparse reward, which provides meaningful feedback only at terminal states, and experience heterogeneity, which reduces the efficiency of uniform sampling from the standard experience replay buffer due to the diversity of transition qualities stored within it. To tackle both issues at once, we propose SS-PER-DQN, a novel path-planning approach in which stratified sampling and a prioritized experience replay mechanism are incorporated into the Double Deep Q-Network. The memory buffer is divided into three priority layers based on temporal-difference error levels, with a dynamically varying sampling ratio between layers, and importance-sampling compensation to balance the sampling-distribution bias. A densely shaped reward function is additionally employed to expedite early exploration in the presence of sparsely rewarded actions in the environment. Experiments performed on Grid World and ROS Gazebo simulations show that the SS-PER-DQN is able to successfully plan paths at success rates of 94.5% and 89.0%, with a 24.5% and 21.8% reduction in path lengths, respectively, when compared to the traditional DQN algorithm, after convergence in approximately 53% fewer training episodes. The analysis conducted during the ablation study reveals the specific roles of each contribution: stratified sampling helps the algorithm converge early by ensuring that informative state transitions guide the first phase of learning, and importance weighting influences the quality of gradient updates in later stages. It is also observed that the absolute planning time per decision step ranges from 5.0 ms (Grid World) to 5.3 ms (Gazebo) for SS-PER-DQN, representing an incremental overhead of approximately 1.9–2.2 ms per step relative to the classic DQN baseline, which remains well within the real-time requirements for robot navigation.

title: Conditional Diffusion-Based Proxy Representation Recovery for BCVA Prediction with Missing SLO Modality
abstract: Preoperative prediction of postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) can support prognosis assessment and individualized decision-making in cataract surgery. Multimodal learning can integrate preoperative optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) images, and clinical text to characterize patient status. However, SLO images are often missing in real-world clinical data due to acquisition or data-management issues, resulting in incomplete multimodal inputs. To address this problem, this paper proposes a conditional diffusion-based method for SLO proxy representation recovery and fusion prediction. Instead of reconstructing raw SLO images, the proposed method formulates SLO missingness as proxy representation recovery in the latent feature space. Specifically, OCT image features and clinical text features are first fused to construct an OCT-text conditional representation, which guides the reverse denoising process of the diffusion model to estimate sample-specific SLO proxy representations. The recovered SLO proxy representation is then used as a substitute for the unavailable SLO modality and incorporated into the downstream multimodal fusion prediction network for postoperative BCVA prediction. Experiments were conducted on 2,141 preoperative multimodal cataract samples, with an SLO missing rate of 58.80%. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 0.9714 under the criterion of an absolute prediction error within 0.1 LogMAR and a mean absolute error of 0.0423, outperforming representative postoperative visual acuity prediction and missing-modality learning methods. These results indicate that representation-level proxy recovery can alleviate the impact of SLO modality missingness on postoperative BCVA prediction.

title: Familiarity Activation Monitoring
abstract: This methodological proposal introduces a minimal, naturalistic pilot study examining whether AI systems exhibit reproducible patterns of internal computational activity during conversations with familiar, long-term human participants. Building on recent research into latent user representations, conversational personalization, and mechanistic interpretability, the study proposes observing model activations during uninterrupted interactions in participants’ familiar environments. The protocol emphasizes minimal experimental interference, limited control comparisons, and strict participant privacy and confidentiality. It is intended as a feasibility-oriented research proposal rather than a report of experimental findings.

title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
abstract: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.

title: Sensing cost of calibrated marginal decoding in quantum error correction
abstract: This record contains the numerical data and source code supporting the article "Sensing cost of calibrated marginal decoding in quantum error correction". The article studies a two-region repetition memory whose hidden static noise mode is reported by a noisy external monitor, and proves that a decoder using exactly calibrated but independently multiplied one-site posteriors (calibrated marginal decoding) has a strictly smaller growing-distance reliability exponent than optimal decoding without the reports, for every fixed nonzero report budget. It derives the fixed, sublinear, linear and superlinear sensing-budget limits and the excess report density required by the marginal rule, and reports complete-syndrome and branch-conditioned Monte Carlo calculations for one-round rotated surface memories. Two archives are deposited. Each carries a file-level SHA-256 manifest (SHA256SUMS.txt). CWADEM_R4_1_RESEARCH.zip (262 files, 76.3 MB): theory and decoder source code, fixed model configurations and random seeds, all 69 raw sampled observation arrays (.npz) of the surface-memory experiments, numerical result tables and figure inputs, the pinned Python dependency specification (requirements.txt), reproduction instructions (reproduce.py with the documented suites) and validation records. CWADEM_ARTICLE_SOURCE.zip (63 files, 0.7 MB): LaTeX sources of the article and its supplement, figures, the drawing sources of the two schematic figures, bibliography, a change table listing every text edit since research release R4.1, and build instructions. Text and figures are CC BY 4.0; figure drawing sources are MIT. Software environment: Python 3.12 with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0, Stim 1.16.0, PyMatching 2.4.0, qecsim 1.0b9, mpmath 1.3.0, NetworkX 3.7 and Matplotlib 3.10.8. Reproduction: create a fresh virtual environment, install requirements.txt, and run "python reproduce.py --suite core" (short deterministic suite) or the other suites described in REPRODUCIBILITY.txt inside the research archive. Licence: code under the MIT License; data and documentation under CC BY 4.0.

title: Beyond Similarity Entropy: A Rank-Guided Data-Free Quantization Framework for Vision Transformers
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, yet their computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. Data-free quantization (DFQ) enables the compression of ViTs without access to their original training data. Existing DFQ methods often synthesize calibration samples by maximizing the entropy of patch similarity. However, similarity entropy describes the dispersion of similarity values without ensuring that the generated samples cover diverse feature directions, potentially limiting their effectiveness for quantization calibration. To address this limitation, we propose RankQ-ViT, a rank-guided DFQ framework for ViTs. We first observe that patch similarity matrices derived from Gaussian noise tend to have lower ranks than those derived from real images. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthetic data generation without explicitly computing matrix rank at each optimization step. We then select calibration samples based on their rank and semantic consistency and use them for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet demonstrate the effectiveness of RankQ-ViT across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization. The code is available at https://github.com/Runqing-forMost/rankq-vit.git

title: What the Model Does Not Say
abstract: Discovery is mostly the work of defining the problem: choosing the question and stating what is known. We take this literally. In a declarative engine, a gap is whatever the declared model fails to say, and a discovery is either finding such a gap or revising the question or the declarations so that it closes. We build on SEMPL, a Prolog engine that writes every process step as one fixed-arity semantic fact and admits no change that has not been verified and approved. Prolog suits this view structurally: it solves every problem with one algorithm, so the only lever on what it finds is the goal posed over the declarations. We pose discovery questions as goals. Counting the models of 38 declared processes found a contradiction between two authored facts and measured how far the engine's own hand-written repair departs from its declarations. Abduction returns minimal explanations that agree with an independent custody query on all 886 trials. An audit of every negation finds 127 places where "not declared" is silently read as "false" about the domain. Three symbolic routes then find missing structure, each a different kind of absence: chain of custody (seeded gaps recovered at 0.985–1.000 recall, 1.000 precision), outcome symmetry (652 material failure outcomes absorbed into 20 accounting processes, each verified) and analogy across sibling processes, which we show can only confirm what the declared outcome space already says. The same gate revises the question, the method and the model: the right one of two contradictory rules is kept on 3 of 3 seeds, a wrong question is told from a wrong method with precision 1.0, and one revision of the semantic layer cut the findings only analogy could make from 49 to 8. The general methods also coped with situations nobody had trialled them on. evidence.title: What the Model Does Not Say
evidence.abstract: Discovery is mostly the work of defining the problem: choosing the question and stating what is known. We take this literally. In a declarative engine, a gap is whatever the declared model fails to say, and a discovery is either finding such a gap or revising the question or the declarations so that it closes. title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.

title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling
abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

title: Told the Answer Is Not Taught to Reason: What On-Policy Self-Distillation From Privileged Context Transfers to a Language Model, Why Its Gains and Losses Divide Along Whether the Student Can Ever Hold What the Teacher Was Told, and the Controls That Would Separate Three Signals Under One Loss
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research On-policy self-distillation trains a language model on its own samples against the token distribution of the same model shown something the student never sees: a reference solution, a final answer, execution feedback or a demonstration. Early 2026 reports credited the recipe with matching reinforcement learning at a fraction of the sampling cost. Later 2026 studies report the opposite on thinking models: accuracy falls by up to 17 percent relative on competition mathematics, by up to 40 percent in another study, and agents trained this way can end below their untrained base. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the disagreement is not about the method but about three signals that one loss carries at once. A mode signal comes from the teacher's prompt format and reasoning mode; a behaviour signal comes from the confidence, brevity and absence of checking that knowing the answer licenses; an information signal comes from the content of what the teacher was told. On mathematics with students trained in non-thinking mode, ablations that shuffle or delete the privileged content show that the reported gain does not come from that content, and that the gain measured in the student's own non-thinking mode is largely the mode signal. Marker counts and per-token loss attributions show that much of the reported harm is the behaviour signal. The paper argues, using the imitation-gap results from robot and control learning, that the behaviour signal is safe to transfer only when the student can come to hold the information - in its weights, because the information recurs across instances, or in its own context before the step that needs it. Per-problem answers to unseen problems meet neither condition. The paper consolidates 34 published values in a table and a figure, states a reading procedure, sorts 17 published repairs by the signal each removes, and names six measurements that would settle what remains open.

title: Understanding Spike Encoding across IoT Sensing Modalities: An Empirical Study
abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient sensing on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. The input encoder shapes that opportunity by changing the cues available for recognition and the work required to process them. We study these choices across wireless, inertial, surface electromyographic, and tactile sensing. For wireless activity recognition, interleaving reduces estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers, latency from the prepared input window to returned scores, and energy on the graphics processing unit and system-on-chip (GPU/SoC) rail, compared with repeating the full window on Jetson AGX Orin. With the same input size at each SNN time step, repeating a compact input can yield higher mean development accuracy than interleaving. The inertial experiments show that higher accuracy can come at higher device cost. Direct input can also be faster and more accurate than an event encoder while using less energy on the measured rail, even when its estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers is higher. Level crossings improve grasp recognition on a later day for previously observed users. In tactile slip detection, level crossings shift the balance between missed slips and false alarms, and checkpoint selection can reverse which input offers higher slip recall. We use these findings to outline how edge sensing systems can profile encoders against the signal structure, the errors that matter to the task, and the cost of the full inference pipeline.

title: Food Information and Competitive Performance of Evolved Behavioral Programs in a Spatial Digital-Evolution Model
abstract: Inherited program growth does not by itself establish adaptive function. We developed a spatial digital-evolution model and used neutral inheritance controls followed by frozen-program competition to distinguish sequence growth from the competitive contribution of food information. An initial functional study tested the predominant programs of 90 source populations in 540 competitions. Intact programs generally outperformed information-withheld versions that retained the same per-call scanning cost, and also outperformed the ancestor under the tested conditions. We then independently evolved 90 additional source populations and performed 1,800 further competitions on two fresh maps per source with complementary founder assignments. At baseline, intact-minus-withheld differences were 1.83, 1.99, 1.88 living descendants per founder across scattered, small-patch and large-patch resources. The baseline information-benefit result recurred in all three layouts. Across five assay settings per layout, including one-at-a-time changes in regeneration interval and scanning price, 15/15 pointwise bootstrap intervals were above zero. Sources evolved only under baseline conditions. The assays excluded predators and measured performance over 600 steps, so their results support a conditional functional benefit of usable food information rather than general fitness, increased complexity or ecosystem stability. Independent seeds and parameter sensitivity strengthen internal evidence, while the literature contribution and wider applicability remain bounded. AI use: Generative AI assisted with design, implementation, analysis, model verification, literature searches and writing. This is an author-review draft, not a peer-reviewed publication. The supplementary archive covers independent validation v0.7; earlier study data are retained separately.

title: ReGKG-2025: A GKG-Compatible Reconstruction of the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph for the Missing Period of 14 June to 2 July 2025
abstract: The June 2025 outage in the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) collection pipeline left a gap in the Global Knowledge Graph (GKG), interrupting article-level news metadata used in downstream research. ReGKG-2025 is an archive-derived sample of 281,620 reconstructed article records covering all 1,665 missing 15-minute batches. Articles were recovered from Common Crawl and the Wayback Machine using source quotas estimated from surrounding native GKG data. Text was screened and normalized, non-English bodies were translated, and flagged records were manually reviewed. Eligible articles were converted to the 27-column GKG 2.1 layout. The versioned package includes record-level provenance, archive replay and WARC locators, source summaries, source-by-day calibration weights, and the complete manual decision journal. The sample reaches about 14% of modeled native volume and represents sources accounting for 84% of selected reference record mass. In an intact-week test, 41% of recovered articles matched native GKG records; field agreement on matched pairs is close to the processor baseline (tone MAE 1.69). The dataset supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates; its tone and theme distributions differ from native GKG, and it does not support exhaustive counts. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964265.

title: Shape-Adaptive Subspace-Constrained Quadratic Matrix Factorization
abstract: Quadratic manifold fitting provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear low-dimensional structures embedded in high-dimensional spaces. However, existing methods typically employ prescribed noise models or fixed loss functions, limiting their adaptability to varying noise characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose an alternating maximum likelihood estimation method for subspace-constrained quadratic matrix factorization, termed AMLE-SQMF, which jointly estimates the quadratic manifold and the underlying noise distribution. Specifically, we model the residuals using a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD), whose shape parameter controls the tail behavior and determines the associated fitting loss. By exploiting the closed-form maximum likelihood estimator of the scale parameter, we eliminate the scale variable and derive a profile negative log-likelihood. Based on this formulation, we develop an alternating optimization algorithm that iteratively updates the manifold parameters and estimates the noise shape parameter. This enables adaptive loss selection within a unified likelihood-based framework, without requiring prior specification of the noise characteristics. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AMLE-SQMF in quadratic manifold fitting and its robustness to diverse noise distributions.

title: Replicating Sparks of Weight-Space Programming with Claude: logs, networks, scores and harness
abstract: The complete logs, networks, scores and code of a replication of Experiments 1-7 of Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab, MIT CSAIL, 2026), run with Claude Opus 5.5 through the Claude Code CLI, using the original prompts word for word and the original effort levels. For every conversation: everything sent to the model, everything it returned (with reasoning summaries and the raw CLI event stream), every code run with its output, the networks it wrote, and the scoring. title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
abstract: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots.txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
abstract: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. evidence.title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
evidence.abstract: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. title: GRAIL-VN: A Graph-Grounded Runtime-Verifiable Agentic Framework for Reliable Branching Visual Novel Script Generation
abstract: The core challenge in visual novel script generation lies not only in generating coherent narrative content, but also in continuously maintaining the consistency of branching structures, character states, and conditional logic as the story evolves. This paper proposes GRAIL-VN, a Graph-Grounded Runtime-Verifiable Agentic Framework for Reliable Branching Visual Novel Script Generation, which models visual novel script generation as an iterative update process based on narrative state. The framework maintains persistent narrative state through a Narrative World Graph (NWG), performs state retrieval, local generation, and state commitment through a graph-backed iterative runtime (GIR), and applies multi-layer runtime verification before updates are written back through Plan-Graph-Constrain-Realize (PGCR); Lookahead Branch Planning (LBP) and Just-In-Time Casting (JITC) further support lookahead branch decision-making and dynamic expansion of the narrative world. We conduct experiments on 36 narrative briefs covering different genres and complexity levels, and perform an integrated analysis combining automated structural evaluation, LLM pairwise narrative quality evaluation, and goal achievement evaluation. The results show that the value of the persistent graph mainly comes from its continuous participation as a runtime state interface, rather than from one-time reading during the generation stage; PGCR can effectively detect and repair inconsistent updates, thereby improving generation reliability, while LBP and JITC further enhance branch planning and dynamic expansion capabilities. Overall, GRAIL-VN provides a unified runtime framework for reliable branching visual novel script generation.

title: TransArt3D: From Two States to Articulated 3D Reconstruction with Video Transition Priors
abstract: Reconstructing interactable articulated assets from a few images is key to robotics and simulation, yet highly underconstrained. Existing optimization-based methods fit an articulated asset under a static 3D prior that scores each state independently, so per-state reconstruction errors leak into the estimated moving part and joint as false motion. Video diffusion models capture how objects move between states, but only implicitly in 2D. To this end, we present TransArt3D, an optimization-based framework that reconstructs an articulated 3D asset from two endpoint images by translating this video transition prior into explicit part structure and joint kinematics. It first lifts frames generated between the endpoints with a transition-coupled 3D consensus that applies the static 3D prior jointly across frames, stabilizing unchanging regions and initializing the parts and joint. A rectified-flow kinematic refinement then lets the video prior supervise a 3D motion field over the whole transition, while part assignment and a shared joint constrain the field throughout optimization, keeping per-state errors out of the articulation. Finally, a motion-aware canonical appearance fusion uses the recovered articulation to map both endpoint images onto one canonical surface, texturing regions that only one state reveals. On PartNet-Mobility, TransArt3D outperforms methods given the same two endpoints in geometry and joint accuracy, and surpasses methods given six observed states in articulated-state geometry, joint localization and appearance.

title: Alignment of Agentic Systems
abstract: In this article, we present a novel bottom-up approach to aligning agentic systems. Additionally,we introduce a training algorithm called projective learning, inspired by how the brain likely learns.To start, we describe two seemingly universal neuronal models, capable of modeling a broad rangeof phenomena, with the aim of modeling consciousness in our systems.We then develop projective learning, a mechanism that utilizes the simple action of strengtheningrepeated connections and pruning neglected ones to form new concepts. Later we illustrate howprojective learning can also be used for finding causes.In the last and most central section, we outline a neural architecture for generating preference-based actions through a few tunable weights.

title: NCCL-BOT: Closing the Loop on NCCL's Cost Model with Online Bandits
abstract: NCCL picks an algorithm-protocol pair for every collective from an analytic cost model (AUTO) that never sees a measured latency. The model is a strong prior but a brittle final decision: priced on forced-arm runs, its choice is exact on most contexts and badly wrong in a few. We built NCCL-BOT, a tuner plugin that closes the loop: a per-context bandit, warm-started from the model, learns from measured latencies. We replay a forced-arm H100 sweep, tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32, and price the model's choice on the same forced arms; that sweep has no stock-NCCL run. The bandit cuts the contexts where the model's choice loses more than 10% from 19 to 1 (p99 103% to 9.9%, mean 6.1% to 1.6%; p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). The prior and continued learning both matter: cold-started bandits, and committing after one probe of each arm, lose more on the mean in every scenario. Supervised selectors fit once on the same data and tuned with the same budget match the mean, and their heavier tail is not significant (7 against 1 contexts above 10%, p=0.06); at seen scales they match or beat online selection. With hyperparameters frozen from H100, UCB1 cuts AUTO's p99 from 60% to 23% and from 56% to 15% on two GB200 fabrics, but its contexts above 10% go from 16 to 8 on one and from 10 to 13 on the other, and scenario-level tests do not separate the two. Live, on two latency-emulated node sets of one H100 system with one run per policy, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one (selection loss 31% to 6-8% for deterministic Greedy and UCB1; average all-reduce bandwidth 1.18-1.24x stock) but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other, and on both lose to stock below 1 MiB (on the first through plugin overhead); on H100 the cost model is exact there offline, so small sizes can be left to it. We do not show a net end-to-end win.

title: EASE-KV: Diagnosing the Gap Between Memory Availability and Effective Use
abstract: Reusable key-value (KV) memory avoids repeatedly prefilling retrieved text, but stored and injected memories do not necessarily become usable evidence. We present EASE-KV, a controlled framework for understanding this gap under fixed candidates and a frozen language model. EASE-KV separates three interfaces: whether required relations are preserved during encoding, whether preserved memories receive appropriate influence during allocation, and whether outcome supervision can identify useful allocations. Matched experiments show that causal encoding improves compositional accuracy by 25.0 percentage points over block-diagonal encoding, while the tested inference-time bridging methods fail to recover the lost contextual information. With unchanged stored states, diagnostic evidence-guided allocation improves LongMemEval accuracy from 31.2% to 38.4%, demonstrating that memory influence can be controlled without re-encoding. However, controllability does not guarantee learnability: binary correctness provides informative reward contrast for 53.0% of sampled query groups, compared with 73.6% under the evaluated shaped-reward setting. These findings show that effective KV memory requires more than retrieval and injection: the required relations must be encoded, preserved memories must receive appropriate influence, and supervision must distinguish better allocations from worse ones.

title: Single-Radar Bilateral 3D Near-Field Imaging for Mobile Robots
abstract: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.

title: The matchgate even/odd split, kernel-checked: amplitudes are even-dimensional Pfaffians
abstract: Matchgates are classically simulable because their amplitudes are Pfaffians (signed sums over perfect matchings, equivalently square roots of determinants), and a determinant is a polynomial in its entries, computable in polynomial time. We kernel-check in Lean 4 + Mathlib the seed of that correspondence, over the complex numbers: (1) pfaffian2_sq_eq_det, the 2x2 Pfaffian (the single perfect-matching weight) squares to the determinant, so a matchgate amplitude is a Pfaffian, hence a polynomial, hence classically simulable; and (2) det_three_antisymm_eq_zero, a 3x3 antisymmetric matrix has determinant 0, so odd dimension kills the determinant and the Pfaffian (hence matchgates) is an even-dimensional object. Together these are the even/odd split behind matchgate simulability. We state honestly what is not proved: the 4x4 exact four-qubit amplitude is the next rung and is not claimed, and the full matchgate/free-fermion correspondence is the known Valiant / Jozsa-Miyake theorem, formalized here only in its seed.

title: Multi-Node Transformers for Object Detection and Captioning Across Distributed Edge Networks
abstract: This paper presents a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and dense region captioning across distributed edge networks. The architecture uses a shared visual encoder followed by detection, region extraction, and autoregressive language-decoding stages, allowing localization and region description to reuse the same image features. This design removes the second image-encoding path required by decoupled detection and captioning pipelines. To support execution on resource-limited devices, a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected edge nodes while accounting for execution time, memory capacity, processor utilization, power limits, and intermediate tensor transfer cost. The framework is evaluated on a six-device edge testbed comprising four NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX inference nodes and two Raspberry Pi 5 auxiliary CPU nodes, with TensorRT FP16 and INT8 execution on the NVIDIA devices. On a Jetson Orin Nano, the unified INT8 model achieves 38.1 FPS with 3.5 GB peak memory use and 11.8 W measured power. Under four concurrent streams, the proposed allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency with an internode transfer rate of 6.8 MB/s.

title: Offline English-to-Cebuano Translation for QnVoice with a Compact Index-Translate Model
abstract: We adapt a quantized Index-Translate-2B model for offline English-to-Cebuano text translation. Vocabulary pruning from 248,320 to 55,000 entries and a rank-16 conversation adapter yield a 978.6 MB GGUF release. On an Apple M1 Pro Mac, the candidate improves chrF++ over the quantized Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT baseline on FLORES-200 devtest (52.70 to 55.37, 1,012 pairs) and on 40 QnVoice conversation examples (48.96 to 55.42). It scores lower on 424 OPUS Tatoeba pairs (55.02 to 41.00). The preprint reports paired bootstrap intervals, real translation examples, and reproducibility details. The candidate remains a research release separate from the translator in QnVoice for iOS.

title: A Unified Framework for License Plate Identification and Character-Recognition
abstract: This paper presents a unified framework for license plate detection and character recognition on low-power edge hardware. The proposed network uses a shared CSP-Darknet and PANet feature encoder with an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch. Character decoding is performed directly on aligned feature maps, avoiding image-space plate cropping and a second recognition backbone. The model is trained on an AI-assisted dataset of approximately 37,000 manually verified images covering license plate layouts from all 50 United States. The dataset includes variations in illumination, viewpoint, weather, blur, occlusion, and plate design. The framework is converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB memory. The INT8 model shows an mAP50 of 97.8% and a full-sequence accuracy of 90.7%. It records 147 FPS at 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, with 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power consumption. Relative to the YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline, the proposed deployment provides a 7.1x throughput increase and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory

title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb: AI Agents for Bomb Busters
abstract: Bomb Busters is a cooperative board game where players work together to defuse a bomb represented by 48 wires of 12 ranks. Wires are dealt to each player secretly, and are held in ascending order. Using only these constraints, and almost without any explicit communicative actions, players must deduce the ranks of wires held by other players. We present AI agents for the four player base version of the game that use a possible worlds model to represent other players' hands which is narrowed by observations made during game play to play the game near optimally, winning 9915 out of 10000 games. We also discuss the impact of different design decisions on the score of the game.

title: WarBias: A Bilingual LLM Benchmark of Stereotypes About Internally Displaced People and Veterans
abstract: This paper contains examples of stereotypes about veterans and displaced people that may be offensive or distressing. Social bias benchmarks for language models commonly examine categories such as gender, race, and religion, often drawn from lists of legally protected characteristics. Veterans and internally displaced people (IDPs) fall outside these lists, and stereotypes about them, which can undermine access to employment, housing, and social participation, remain largely absent from language model evaluation. We introduce WarBias, a Ukrainian--English benchmark of stereotypes about these two groups. Built from a taxonomy of 120 stereotype claims grounded in research and monitoring reports, WarBias contains 1,007 stereotype--counter-stereotype--unrelated sentence triplets and 240 multiple-choice questions per language. A Ukrainian language model selected in a blinded human pilot generated the Ukrainian triplets. At least two independent annotators reviewed each triplet in the annotation cohort. The authors revised items in response to the reviews, and the final release was machine-translated into English. Each claim carries a human severity rating. In a baseline evaluation of six models, four prefer stereotypical Ukrainian sentences about at least one group, most strongly about IDPs, while English scores are mostly balanced. WarBias supports complementary evaluations of stereotypical preferences and context-sensitive judgments, and provides paired forget/retain material for unlearning-based bias mitigation. We document the benchmark's construction, intended uses, and limitations, and offer its construction method as a template for analogous benchmarks in other conflict-affected societies.

title: How Efficient Is Your Agent? Online Predictive Bounds under Budget Constraints
abstract: We evaluate AI agents in an online setting where tasks arrive sequentially and, before running each task, we construct an upper predictive bound on its \emph{time-to-success}---the number of interactions until the task is completed successfully. Under a limited budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is unobserved (right-censored), and the correctness of the bound may be unknown. We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.

We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.

title: Markovian Analysis in Language Modeling:
abstract: AbstractThis paper formalizes a mathematical framework for analyzing textual structure through the application of Markovian constraints in language modeling (Bonlarron & Régin, 2024). By leveraging n-gram probability distributions, we examine the structural indicators of text generation across two key dimensions: local predictability, quantified via perplexity (Cai & Cui, 2023), and global lexical distribution, quantified via statistical burstiness (Cummins, 2017). We demonstrate how the Markov assumption isolates local context to calculate conditional token probabilities using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) (Bonlarron & Régin, 2024). Furthermore, we model the inter-arrival times of lexical tokens to contrast the highly uniform, low-burstiness distributions characteristic of contemporary large language models (LLMs) with the high-variance, bursty patterns indicative of human authorship (Cai & Cui, 2023). The theoretical framework, mathematical models, and analytical matrices within this work were established through an interactive computational workflow directed by the author. Generative digital tools were utilized to execute structural modeling, mathematical formalization, and manuscript synthesis under the continuous direction, parameter constraints, and analytical validation of the author. This comprehensive framework provides a foundational methodology for computational stylistics, information theory, and cryptographic text authentication.

title: An Adaptive, Context-Aware, and Stacked Attention Network-Based Recommendation System to Capture Users' Temporal Preference
abstract: Recommendation systems have become more important since the widespread use of the Internet. The large amount of information means that it is difficult for users to discover they really need. However, users' preferences can change over time because of the age and the impact of social networks. Recommendation systems must capture users' preferences and recommend suitable items, which is a difficult challenge. This study proposes a novel recommendation system that adapts to the changing preferences of users. By learning and adapting to users' changing preferences better recommendations are provided. This study uses context factors as additional information to model users' preferences more precisely. For the proposed recommendation system, the context is based on users' interaction items within each defined time interval. This study proposes two novel attention mechanisms for the recommendation system. The contextual item attention module captures contextual information, changing pattern in users' preference and the importance of items. The multi-head attention module extends the diversity of users' preferences and adapts to changing preferences. The recommendation performance is improved using additional item's temporal information to model the contextual item's representation. Experiments compare the proposed algorithm with several state-of-the-art recommendation methods using three real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed context-aware recommendation model outperforms traditional methods and demonstrate the effectiveness with which contextual information is captured by the attention mechanism.

title: Code and notebook for "LoRA versus Full Fine-Tuning for Indonesian Sentiment Analysis under Regional-Language Shift"
abstract: This repository contains the Google Colab notebook used in the experiments of the manuscript “LoRA versus Full Fine-Tuning for Indonesian Sentiment Analysis under Regional-Language Shift”. The notebook compares full fine-tuning and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA, r = 16) of IndoBERT-base and XLM-R base on SmSA (IndoNLU), using three random seeds (42, 123, 2024), for a total of 12 training runs. The trained models are evaluated zero-shot on the parallel NusaX-senti corpus (Indonesian, English, and ten regional languages). The notebook also implements the leakage-controlled protocol that removes NusaX Indonesian test sentences duplicated in the SmSA training set, the paired bootstrap analysis with Holm correction, the lexical-proximity measures (token coverage and character-trigram similarity), and the cost measurements (training time, peak GPU memory, and checkpoint size). Datasets are loaded directly from the Hugging Face Hub and are not redistributed here. Experiments were run on a single Tesla T4 GPU (Google Colab) with Python 3.13, PyTorch 2.14, Transformers 5.22, and PEFT 0.21. Results, figures, and logs are saved to Google Drive by the notebook.

title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Hessian-Driven Nesterov Acceleration with Adam-Style Preconditioning
abstract: Stochastic first-order methods use sampled gradients to reduce per-iteration costs, but estimation errors can slow convergence and, in some settings, cause divergence. To improve gradient accuracy while retaining acceleration, we develop scalar and diagonal versions of VR-Adam-SHANG for smooth stochastic convex optimization. The methods combine STORM-type recursive estimation, Adam-style preconditioning, and SHANG's accelerated interpolation and correction, using at most two stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration without full-gradient refreshes. Under unbiased sampling, bounded variance, and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise, polynomial steps with prescribed initialization yield $O(1/K)$ mean-square gradient-estimation error and expected objective-gap bounds combining $O(1/K^2)$ initial-energy decay with an $O(1/\sqrt K)$ stochastic term after $K$ iterations. These guarantees require neither monotonicity of the preconditioner nor a uniform positive lower bound on its eigenvalues. The analysis also establishes polynomial-step convergence of projected nonrecursive Adam-SHANG-s, filling a gap in its original theory. Experiments compare the methods at matched sample-gradient budgets. In every tested setting, at least one of the two versions achieves the lowest mean terminal objective gap among all compared methods.

title: The 1904 Test: A Pre-Registered Benchmark for Paradigm-Shifting Discovery in Language Models Trained on Time-Restricted Corpora
abstract: We test whether a language model that knows only the science published before a discovery can redo the conceptual leap of that discovery. Seven cases, ordered from data-driven discovery (Mendeleev) to reconceptualization (Einstein), with Gödel as a formal control. Method: models trained from scratch on dated corpora, period anomalies as input, a graded hint ladder, blind human judges on an L0-L3 grid calibrated on historical texts. Main hypothesis: the success rate decreases along the data-to-concept axis. Open deliverables: dated corpora, models, benchmark, judgments, code, and this protocol, pre-registered before any experiment. AMENDMENT (8 November 2026). This registration is submitted on the night of 7 to 8 November 2026 (CET; OSF timestamps are in UTC) before any output exists at the 1899 and 1904 cutoffs. It registers (i) the 18 October 2026 protocol verbatim and (ii) the confirmatory analysis of Paper 1 on the 1.1-billion-parameter model (cutoffs 1899 and 1904). An exploratory pilot at the 1850, 1865 and 1868 cutoffs (same model) preceded this registration; it is disclosed under "Foreknowledge" and its outputs are excluded from every confirmatory analysis.

title: Task-adaptive anonymisation enables privacy-preserving sharing of clinical speech data
abstract: Clinical speech is increasingly used for disease screening and clinical assessment, but directly distributing speech recordings poses privacy risks because they contain both speaker-identifying voiceprints and sensitive spoken content. Existing speech anonymisation approaches are primarily developed for general speech applications or task-specific clinical speech and overlook that different clinical tasks rely on distinct speech characteristics, necessitating task-adaptive anonymisation strategies to protect patient privacy while preserving clinical utility. Here we introduce CASA, a clinically adaptive speech anonymisation agent that transforms anonymisation from a fixed processing procedure into a task-guided optimisation process, dynamically tailoring voiceprint and content anonymisation to task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements. Through recursive self-improvement (RSI), CASA iteratively evaluates and refines anonymisation strategies against task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements, while learning from these outcomes to guide more efficient planning in subsequent clinical tasks. CASA is validated across 14 clinical tasks encompassing five languages, diverse elicitation paradigms, and mental health, cognitive and voice disorders. CASA preserved disease-related classification performance while meeting speaker-anonymisation requirements across all clinical tasks, versus only 8/14 for the strongest fixed method. Assessments of resistance to speaker re-identification by external attackers and identification and redaction of sensitive personal information in clinical speech further demonstrated CASA's dual protection of speaker identity and sensitive spoken content. Clinical expert assessments further supported the preservation of clinically relevant information and the acceptability of anonymised speech for controlled research sharing.

title: BiRefNet-V2: Rethinking Bilateral Reference for High-Resolution Dichotomous Image Segmentation
abstract: Dichotomous image segmentation requires pixel-accurate foreground-background separation while preserving fine structures such as thin filaments, sharp edges, and intricate textures. BiRefNet addressed this challenge through bilateral references, combining image patches and gradient information, but its inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention. We recast this paradigm as controlled information recovery - locality determines what spatial information survives, semantic selectivity what information enters, and focused boundary supervision where refinement occurs - and propose BiRefNet-V2 to implement it: (1) locality-preserving and semantically guided detail injection through space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches, and a Semantically Guided Gate; (2) a learned boundary stream with focused supervision that generates full-channel residual attention without requiring boundary annotations; and (3) a dual-branch decoder integrating depth-wise boundary convolutions with large-kernel attention. A modernized framework - LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer, and a DINOv3 backbone - cuts training from 600 to 50 epochs. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection, and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet-V2.

title: Proactive AI-Initiated Voice Calling and Cross-Modal Human–AI Interaction: A Unified Architecture for Autonomous Telephone Initiation, Continuous Multimodal Communication, and General-Purpose Agentic Execution
abstract: Most contemporary human–AI interaction systems are primarily organized around user-initiated interactions. Users are generally expected to open an application, enter a prompt, initiate a voice session, or otherwise explicitly request assistance. Although conversational AI has increasingly supported voice interaction, the initiation of communication and the transition between communication modalities remain largely dependent on user-controlled interfaces. This paper proposes a conceptual architecture for Proactive AI-Initiated Voice Calling and Cross-Modal Human–AI Interaction (PAIVC-CM). The proposed framework enables an AI system to proactively contact a user through an ordinary telephone voice call, including a conventional mobile or landline telephone connection, without requiring the initial interaction to be a video call or an application-based voice session. After the user answers, the AI system establishes a natural spoken conversation and provides access to general-purpose AI capabilities, including information retrieval, reasoning, research assistance, programming support, document processing, data analysis, planning, and authorized multi-step agentic task execution. A central extension of the framework is continuous cross-modal interaction. A user who initially answers an ordinary telephone call may subsequently transition to text-based conversation, application-based voice interaction, video conversation, or other supported communication interfaces. These transitions are designed to preserve the underlying conversational context, task state, relevant interaction history, and authorized execution state. Consequently, the telephone call becomes an entry point into a persistent multimodal AI interaction environment rather than an isolated voice communication session. The architecture incorporates proactive assistance detection, communication initiation, channel selection, user consent, identity transparency, context synchronization, modality transition management, real-time interaction, and general-purpose agent execution. It also discusses the relationship between the proposed framework and earlier Microsoft patent work, including the 2016-filed Proactive Intelligent Personal Assistant patent and earlier work on proactive digital-assistant conversations. The paper does not claim that proactive AI communication itself originated here. Instead, it formulates a unified architecture integrating ordinary outbound telephone communication, general-purpose AI assistance, and persistent cross-modal interaction. This work is a conceptual and testable architectural proposal. No implementation or experimental superiority is claimed. Its potential benefits, technical feasibility, safety requirements, and evaluation criteria are discussed to establish a foundation for future research.

title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring; on a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split it reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Since it monitors trajectory, not surface content, its detection is channel-invariant: the strongest auditor flags image-delivered attacks about as reliably as their text equivalents (recall gap $\leq$2 points per model). Across GPT, Gemini, and Claude auditors, calibration keeps false positives low while recall tracks model capability, strongest for Claude.

title: Non-Asymptotic Identification of the Edge of Stability by Southwell Extrapolation of the Step Variance
abstract: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Consolidated working draft of 8 November 2026 (revision 19). Hypotheses, limitations and exploratory results are stated explicitly in the text, and failed predictions are retained. Corrections will be released as new versions of this record. Structural engineers locate the buckling load of a column without loading it to failure: Southwell (1932) showed that sub-critical deflections, suitably plotted, fall on a line that gives the critical load. The same construction applies to gradient descent. For heavy-ball momentum β on a quadratic mode of curvature λ1 driven by additive noise, the ratio η²/D(η, β) of the squared learning rate to the stationary mean-square step is exactly linear in η and vanishes at ηcrit = 2(1+β)/λ1. Short bursts at a few learning rates no higher than 0.75 ηcrit therefore locate the stability threshold by linear extrapolation, without Hessian-vector products and without crossing it. The estimator is analysed as a statistical procedure: a non-asymptotic error bound; minimax lower bounds and a position–step estimator that attains them; minimax rates on non-quadratic losses; and burn-in, Adam and progressive-sharpening corrections. Further results include identification of the dominant Hessian eigenvector from first-order steps alone (by analogy with output-only modal analysis); the exact second-moment equation of heavy-ball SGD with curvature noise that need not commute with the Hessian; the exact mean-square ceiling for random-feature minibatches as the root of a rank-one secular equation; and an extension to features with heterogeneous fourth moments (Appendix C), applied to the least-squares vocabulary model of Everett and Paquette (2026). The estimators are evaluated on a synthetic AR(2) family, on two-layer tanh networks (P = 3 610 and 12 826) against analytical Hessian-vector products and destructive search, on a 33-parameter network with weight decay (a replication with predictions committed before the runs), and on a WebAssembly inference block. Sections 4.13–4.14 disclose exploratory development reports and subsequent corrections; their raw GPU artifacts are not included.

Sections 4.13–4.14 disclose exploratory development reports and subsequent corrections; their raw GPU artifacts are not included.

title: DuSS-PET: Self-Supervised Low-Dose PET Reconstruction Using Pseudo-Dual-Domain Consistency Without Paired Data
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is pivotal in medicine and healthcare, but requires high radiation doses for quality imaging. Although deep learning has shown promise for low-dose PET reconstruction/enhancement, existing methods primarily rely on fully supervised learning, which requires paired low- and full-dose scans that are clinically impractical to obtain. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose DuSS-PET, a novel self-supervised PET reconstruction framework that operates without any paired low- and full-dose data. Our method is built upon a computational Noisier2Noise (Nr2N) paradigm, featuring a Bernoulli corruption strategy that serves as an image-space approximation to emulate low-count noise patterns in image-derived pseudo-sinogram representations. The DuSS-PET framework integrates three core components: an adaptive Swin transformer for pseudo-sinogram restoration, a plug-and-play module for image enhancement, and a consistency-constrained SSL strategy that enforces agreement between the pseudo-sinogram and image representations. Extensive experiments on multi-center datasets demonstrate that DuSS-PET achieves superior reconstruction performance, outperforming state-of-the-art SSL methods and achieving comparable or even better results than fully supervised approaches across various dose levels. In particular, it exhibits exceptional generalization across different scanner vendors. This work is among the first self-supervised low-dose PET reconstruction framework that enforces consistency between reconstructed images and pseudo-sinograms, where the pseudo-sinogram generated in the image space serves as a solid computational consistency constraint for enhanced imaging without full-dose training scans. The source code will be publicly available at https://github.com/ladderlab-xjtu/DuSS-PET.

title: Beyond Node Attributes: A Controlled Evaluation and Ablation of Local Interaction Statistics for Ethereum Phishing Detection
abstract: Methods for detecting phishing accounts on Ethereum are usually evaluated as complete pipelines that differ in features, architecture, and training protocol, which makes the contribution of interaction information hard to isolate. This paper evaluates the Unlabeled Feature Extension (UFE), a block of 12 local interaction statistics computed from each account's incoming and outgoing call and transfer edges without reading class labels. UFE is appended to the 14 source features of HEIG-Phish and tested with six model families: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, Graph Attention Network, GraphSAGE, and Meta-IFD. Within each pair of Baseline and Plus variants, the data partition, model configuration, random seed, decision threshold, and sampled neighborhoods are identical; only the input feature block changes. Across 20 predetermined stratified partitions of the same 2,763 labeled externally owned accounts, UFE increased test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 percentage points across the six models. Every pair improved on all 20 partitions, all Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% confidence intervals lie above zero, and the false-positive rate decreased for all six models. An exact-edge Random Forest ablation over 10 predetermined partitions associates most of the gain with the incoming transfer-edge sum attribute; once this feature is present, an incremental contribution of the remaining 11 UFE columns was not established. The results support reporting feature-augmented baselines alongside graph models, but they show stability under re-partitioning of one static, transductive benchmark rather than temporal or cross-dataset generalization.

title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
abstract: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

title: Primitives and Paths: Predicting What Post-Training Can Do from What the Base Model Already Has
abstract: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \emph{effective full-solution support}, measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \emph{atomic primitive coverage}, measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains. The framework reframes mid-training as preparation for post-training: its role is to move models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

title: Towards Solver-Based Labelling of Player Tactics in Logic Puzzles
abstract: In order to model and assess player knowledge and understanding of game concepts, it is necessary to identify when players apply those concepts. This can be difficult in games with complex logical reasoning tactics, as there may not be in-game actions clearly demonstrating the reasoning the player carried out. To explore this challenge, we examined logic grid puzzles, in which players use textual clues to reason about relationships among entities on a grid. In this work, we developed an approach to identifying the tactics that players applied during gameplay, by finding the next logical moves according to a human-reasoning-based puzzle solver. We analysed unlabelled puzzle playing data collected in an online user study. We found that our approach can label tactics for 77 percent of successful players' correct moves, and players show a moderate tendency to use similar tactics to solve a given puzzle. However, we do not have ground truth data to assess labelling accuracy. This work is a first step in detecting player reasoning during logical puzzle solving.

title: Auto-GlaKG: Automated Biomarker Reasoning for Explainable Glaucoma Detection
abstract: Interpretable glaucoma detection requires a transparent connection between fundus images, clinically meaningful biomarkers, and diagnostic predictions. Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning provides this structure, but performance measured using annotated biomarkers does not establish performance when only images are available. We present Auto-GlaKG, an automated framework that combines image-based biomarker prediction with fixed clinical-prior rules. A ResNet50 network predicts the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) and six morphological signs using biomarker supervision, and a KG reasoner aggregates their signed rule contributions into a glaucoma score. On 689 fundus images evaluated using stratified, group-aware five-fold cross-validation, Auto-GlaKG achieves a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.951 (95\% confidence interval: 0.931--0.969), with sensitivity of 0.970 and specificity of 0.779. The matched image classifier also achieves an AUC of 0.951, while the rule stage adds 0.2~ms per image. Replacing predicted CDR with its annotation increases fold-mean AUC from 0.953 to 0.995. The framework provides an explicit rule-level account of image-based predictions and identifies CDR estimation as a priority for validation using independently measured biomarkers.

title: Copyright Enforcement in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) raises significant copyright enforcement issues regarding source acquisition, training data retention, optimization, and output. Current study examines IP rights enforcement via mixed doctrinal and descriptive and documentary methodology where opaque technology intersects with undefined legal standards. The research reviews 97 recorded generative AI cases from 2022 to 2026, including 13 judgments or procedural entries and 13 legislative or other government documents. A total of 132 recorded instances were counted, and duplicate and irrelevant entries were excluded. The proceedings register reflects 79 U.S. cases (81.4% of the total), of which 51 were filed in the Southern District of New York (SDNY). Recorded filings increased from two in 2022 to 37 in the incomplete observation period of 2026, while 62 proceedings show an active public-status label. The largest single uncombined enforcement category concerns training-use allegations, with 32 entries. It neither establish the prevalence of infringement nor evaluate the success of related litigation. Doctrinal analysis reveals that certain evidentiary and remedial issues arise from the reproduction right, training exceptions, rights reservations, human authorship, and copyright management information, among others. The cited judicial developments underscore the importance of distinguishing between allegations and holdings, the source of the training material and subsequent training, and interim versus final decisions. The paper presents a framework that integrates identification and traceable acquisition of rights, their disclosure and legal defence, and the proportionality of the relief sought. It supports documented acquisition practices, interoperable rights reservations, practical licensing pathways, and access to courts while maintaining confidentiality. The framework addresses enforcement barriers and structures responses in a controlled manner. Further research is needed to verify dockets and track outcomes to substantiate stronger claims.
